results.summary: PiMAC is a pipelined multiply-and-accumulate unit that computes a*b+c for 4-bit unsigned inputs. It uses a classic shift-and-add multiplication method, with the partial products computed across pipeline stages and the result available after a latency of three clock cycles. The design is generated with SpinalHDL and exposes a, b, and c on input pins and the 8-bit result on output pins. It is a small arithmetic building block intended for educational or integration purposes, with no external hardware required beyond the digital interface.

This is an 8-bit successive-approximation-register analog-to-digital converter that samples a differential input onto a capacitor array and uses a strong-arm comparator and asynchronous binary-search logic to produce a two's-complement digital output. It requires a 4 MHz clock, an enable signal, and differential analog inputs with a common mode around VDD/2; the conversion-done signal indicates when the output is valid. Silicon test reports indicate it works, but both inputs must be above about 0.6 V for reliable operation, and a common mode of 0 V will cause the comparator to fail. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog block with detailed documentation and measured silicon results.

This design implements a 24-hour digital clock with separate BCD outputs for two hour digits and two minute digits. It uses a 1 MHz reference clock and provides a set button to cycle through the digits and a pulse input to advance the selected digit. External hardware includes three push buttons, a 1 MHz signal generator, and four 7-segment BCD decoders to display the time. The design is a straightforward clock with no unusual features or silicon test results reported.

This project is a UART transceiver for 8-bit data frames with little-endian transmit and receive signals. The documentation is essentially empty, with no description of the implementation, testing procedure, or required external hardware. The pin names suggest a standard UART interface, but no further details are provided. Because of the lack of documentation, it is not possible to say more about its operation or notable characteristics.

Tiny ALU is a simple 4-bit arithmetic logic unit extracted from a larger GPU design. It takes two 4-bit operands and a 2-bit arithmetic mux selection, and produces a 4-bit output; the testbench only exercises the addition function. The design is intended as a small, self-contained submission while the author works on a more complex GPU project. No external hardware is required, and no silicon test results are reported.

This is a multi-digit counter with configurable maximum values and carry-over behavior, built from modified 2-bit up/down counters. It supports two digits, with outputs serialized for 7-segment displays via external 8-bit shift registers such as the HC595. Operation requires three push buttons for digit control and limit refresh, plus three switches for mode selection, and it provides shift-clock outputs for the shift registers. The design is intended for educational use and includes no silicon test results.

The James Retro Byte 8 is an 8-bit microprocessor built from the ground up following the nand2tetris course. It requires external SPI storage for ROM and RAM, with pin mappings compatible with the spi-ram-emu project, and uses a 24-bit addressing mode. The design was tested with a simple repeating output program and works, but further testing with more complex programs and the spi-ram-emu is planned. It is notable for being a complete CPU implementation on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

This is an Intel 8080-compatible CPU core intended to run software such as Microsoft BASIC or CP/M. It requires an external RP2040 to simulate RAM and I/O, and exposes a bus handshake interface along with debug and interrupt signals. The documentation is minimal, with testing procedures still to be determined, and no silicon test results are provided. The design is notable for targeting a classic 8-bit instruction set on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

This analog design implements ReLU and sigmoid activation functions for neuromorphic computing. It provides two analog input-output pairs, with the ReLU output equal to the input when positive and zero otherwise, and the sigmoid output representing a probability for binary classification. External hardware includes a voltage source connected to the analog inputs, typically from an artificial neural network. The documentation is very brief and provides no test results or detailed circuit information.

This is a two-player Pong game implemented in Verilog for a 640x480 VGA display. It uses two rotary encoders for paddle control and outputs VGA signals through a TinyVGA Pmod or similar. The game logic handles ball movement, collision detection, and scoring, and it can be simulated with Verilator and SDL2. The design is a complete game on a single tile and requires external encoders and a VGA interface.
